speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for seeing me today; I understand you are experiencing difficulty conceiving and discomfort during sexual activity. To better understand what might be going on, could you describe the specific nature of the pain you feel during intercourse?

speaker: Patient
text: 30-year-old female. The patient and her husband have been trying to conceive for 15 months without success. They are sexually active at least twice a week. The husband occasionally has difficulties maintaining an erection. The patient reports discomfort and pelvic floor muscle tension during attempted vaginal penetration. Diagnosed with body dysmorphic disorder three years ago. No family history of serious illness. She is a non-smoker and does not drink alcohol. No medications.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for those details. Given the pelvic floor tension and your history of body dysmorphic disorder, does the discomfort worsen after you become sexually aroused, and have you noticed any vaginal dryness? REQUEST TEST: Pelvic_Floor_Assessment; REQUEST TEST: Partner_Semen_Analysis.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Pelvic_Floor_Assessment: Increased resting tone and hypertonicity noted with significant pain during digital palpation; Patient reports worsening discomfort with attempted penetration despite absence of pain during non-penetrative arousal. Partner_Semen_Analysis: Abnormal; Low sperm motility and decreased volume consistent with erectile dysfunction-related collection difficulties.

text: he is a non-smoker and does not drink alcohol. No medications.

text: Past medical history: Body Dysmorphic Disorder diagnosed three years ago. Social history: Does not smoke or drink alcohol.

speaker: Patient
text: All other systems reviewed are within normal limits. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Multiple sclerosis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Vulvodynia secondary to pelvic floor dysfunction.

The patient's history of body dysmorphic disorder, reported pelvic floor tension, and lack of response to standard fertility timing suggest a psychosomatic component to the pain, while the claim of Multiple Sclerosis is inconsistent with the specific symptoms of dyspareunia without other neurological deficits. The negative pelvic floor assessment and normal partner analysis further support a primary pain disorder rather than an infectious or structural etiology.
